title: Web crawler
prompt: Design a crawler that fetches about a billion web pages a month to feed a search index, re-crawling pages that change often.

requirements: Functional: start from seed URLs, fetch pages, extract links, store content for indexing, and re-crawl according to how often pages change.
Politeness: obey robots.txt and keep the request rate to any single host low.
Non-functional: scales horizontally and is robust to crawler traps (endless calendars, session IDs in URLs), slow servers and duplicate content.
estimation: 1B pages a month ≈ 385 pages/s on average (1B ÷ 2.6M seconds); design for ~1,000/s.
At ~100 KB per page that is ~100 TB of raw HTML a month before compression.
Bandwidth: 385 pages/s × 100 KB ≈ 38.5 MB/s ≈ 300 Mbit/s on average.
Seen-URL set: 10B URLs × 8-byte fingerprints ≈ 80 GB, shardable in memory or on SSD; a Bloom filter needs far less at a small false-positive rate.
api: Internal, not public: addSeeds(urls) and an admin view of crawl stats per host.
Frontier: enqueue(url, priority, notBefore) and next(worker) → a URL whose host may be fetched now.
Output: write (url, fetchedAt, status, contentHash, body) to the page store and emit an event for the indexer.
data: Frontier: a queue per host plus a priority structure ordered by each host’s next allowed fetch time.
url_state(fingerprint, last_fetched, last_changed, content_hash, next_due) drives re-crawls.
Page bodies in blob storage keyed by URL hash and fetch time; robots.txt cached per host with a TTL.
design: Scheduler → URL frontier → fetchers (async I/O, caching DNS resolver) → parser → URL filter and dedup → back into the frontier.
Fetched pages go to the page store and onto an index stream.
Partition the frontier by host hash, so one worker group owns each host and politeness is a local decision.
deepDives: Politeness: each host queue has a next-allowed time (a few seconds apart, or robots.txt crawl-delay). Workers only take hosts whose time has passed.
Dedup: normalise URLs (lowercase host, drop fragments, strip known tracking parameters) before fingerprinting; hash content to skip exact copies and use SimHash for near-duplicates.
Re-crawl: estimate each page’s change rate from history; pages that changed recently get shorter intervals, within caps.
bottlenecks: DNS lookups can dominate latency: run a local caching resolver.
Traps: cap URL length, path depth and pages per host per cycle.
A big host cannot be crawled faster without breaking politeness, so throughput comes from crawling many hosts in parallel.
tradeoffs: A Bloom-filter seen-set saves memory, but false positives skip a few new URLs; acceptable for a crawler.
Freshness vs coverage: re-crawl budget competes with discovering new pages.
Host partitioning simplifies politeness but creates skew; rebalance with consistent hashing.

rubric.text: Estimated pages per second, bandwidth and storage.
Designed a frontier that schedules by host and priority.
Handled traps and slow or failing servers.
Explained a re-crawl policy driven by change rate.
Partitioned work across machines and handled host skew.
Quantified Bloom filter or SimHash error trade-offs.
